Well, I still manage to stay in my home, so I do try to keep up with things, but... I suppose I have been putting off things that used to be routine. I actually stopped teaching my craft classes recently. I used to teach crocheting down at the community center on Thursday afternoons. He built a birdhouse once that looked exactly like a miniature Swiss chalet, complete with tiny little window boxes...

Oh, I'm sorry, my mind is just wandering everywhere today. Finances, you asked. I rely a lot more on reminders now, and I've missed some calls and appointments, and family tasks I used to handle carefully. But I'm still in my house, managing as best I can.

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, I am still managing to stay in my home by myself. I don't have a nurse or a housekeeper or anything like that. But I suppose I do put off the things that used to be routine around the house.

Well, my eating has gotten all turned around lately. That's actually part of what made me come in, to be honest. I haven't really been checking the scale to see if I've lost weight, but some days I just forget lunch completely. I told him, I said, \"Arthur, I'm not spending my golden years oiling a countertop.\" So we got the granite. But anyway, yes, the crackers and the sweets... I just stand there at that granite counter and eat them, even though I don't really want them.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble with your memory?\n\nPatient: Memory? Oh, no, I don't think so. I haven't noticed anything like that. My mind is still sharp, thank goodness. I mean, I remember everybody's birthdays without even looking at a calendar. \n\nJust last week I mailed a card to my niece, Susan. She just turned 50. Can you believe it? 50! It feels like just yesterday she was running around my backyard in this little yellow sundress. My sister made that dress for her. She was always so good with a sewing machine. She had one of those old heavy metal Singers, you know the ones? Not like these cheap plastic things they sell nowadays at the big box stores that break if you just look at them wrong. She used to make all our curtains, too, with these beautiful floral patterns. \n\nBut... oh, what were we talking about? Right, my memory. No, I remember things just fine.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any trouble managing your bills?\n\nPatient: Bills? Well, I suppose I've been putting them off a bit. They just sit there in that little brass letter holder on the hall table. Arthur bought me that brass holder at a flea market... oh, it must have been 1982. It really needs a good polishing. Brasso works best for that, but the smell! It's so strong, you have to open all the windows when you use it, and with the breeze we've been having, I just haven't gotten around to it. \n\nBut I still manage to stay in my home, thank goodness. I just... I rely a lot more on reminders now, and I put off things that used to be routine. Like the bills, or... well, I've missed some calls and appointments lately. Even family tasks I used to handle so carefully. I actually stopped teaching my craft classes at the community center, too. We were doing decoupage. Have you ever tried decoupage? You take these beautiful paper napkins—the ones with the delicate floral prints—and you peel them so it's just the very top layer, and you use Mod Podge to stick it onto glass jars or wooden boxes. It makes such lovely gifts. But the glue gets everywhere, and your fingers get all sticky, and... well, I just couldn't keep up with it. \n\nWhat was I saying? Oh, right, the routine things. Yes, I just have to write myself notes for everything these days.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose I have been. It's... mostly in the mornings. I wake up and there's just this heavy, low feeling. It's hard to explain, but it's like all the color has just drained right out of the day before I even have a chance to get out of bed and get dressed. \n\nAnd getting dressed is such a chore anyway. I usually just wrap myself up in this old pink chenille robe. Arthur ordered it for me from the JC Penney catalog years and years ago. Do you remember when they used to mail out those huge catalogs? The Christmas ones were the absolute best, the Wish Books! They were thick as a phone directory. Kids today don't even know what a phone book is, everything is just on those little glowing screens. My neighbor's grandson was over helping her with her yard the other day, and he was just staring at his screen the whole time he was taking a break, didn't even look up to say hello when I went out to get the paper. It's a shame, really, missing out on the whole world around you like that. The birds were singing so beautifully that morning, too. I think it was a cardinal. \n\nBut, oh... what were you asking me? Right, feeling down. Yes, just that heavy feeling when I wake up, like the day is already over before it starts.\n\nDoctor: Do you need help managing your medications?\n\nPatient: Medications? Oh, no, I manage those myself. I have one of those little plastic pill organizers, the ones with the days of the week printed on the lids. Sunday through Saturday. Mine has purple lids, which is nice because purple has always been my favorite color. My bridesmaids all wore lilac dresses at my wedding. They were chiffon, with these delicate little cap sleeves. It was a spring wedding, May of 1971. We had lilac centerpieces, too, and the whole church just smelled heavenly. \n\nThe florist, Mr. Henderson, he was such a dear man. When I was growing up, we had a proper choir with robes, maroon robes with little gold crosses embroidered on the lapels. Mrs. Gable was the choir director, and she was so strict! She used to tap her baton on the music stand if anyone was even a fraction of a beat off. \n\nShe lived in this grand old Victorian house at the end of our street, and she had the most magnificent rose garden. Those awful shiny green bugs, they just eat right through the leaves until they look like lace. No, my friends and family haven't said anything about my memory getting worse.\n\nDoctor: What month is it right now?\n\nPatient: Well, to be perfectly honest, the days just sort of blend together when you're not working, so I'm not entirely sure. I used to keep a very strict calendar, though. Every year, Arthur and I would go down to the mall right after New Year's when all the calendars went on sale. They used to have this little kiosk right in the middle of the concourse, right in front of the Sears. \n\nSears is gone now, of course. It's such a shame, they had the most reliable appliances. We bought a Kenmore washing machine in 1982 and it lasted for over twenty years! The repairman, a lovely fellow named Gary, told me they just don't make the parts out of real metal anymore. Everything is plastic now. Plastic gears, plastic tubs... it's no wonder the landfills are so full. No, she hasn't said she's worried about my memory or my thinking, just the kale.\n\nDoctor: Do you need help with your finances, like paying bills or balancing your checkbook?\n\nPatient: Well, I still manage to stay in my home, so I do try to keep up with things, but... Well, I suppose the honest answer is no, not really. I used to look forward to so many things, you know? My watercolor class, the quilting circle, my Wednesday book club... but now, I'll pack my things up, and I often just leave the bag sitting right by the front door. When Arthur was alive, we used to have a nice iceberg lettuce salad with dinner every night. Just a wedge of iceberg with some Thousand Island dressing and maybe a few croutons. \n\nYou used to be able to get the best croutons at the A&P, they were garlic and herb, and they came in this little foil bag... but A&P closed down ages ago. It turned into a video rental place for a while, Blockbuster, I think it was. We used to rent movies on Friday nights. Arthur loved those old Westerns, John Wayne and Clint Eastwood. I always preferred musicals, like *Singin' in the Rain*. Gene Kelly was such a marvelous dancer, wasn't he? The way he just glided across the screen...\n\nOh, dear me. Sarah. Right. No, she hasn't said she's worried about my memory or my thinking, just the kale.\n\nDoctor: Do you need help with your finances, like paying bills or balancing your checkbook?\n\nPatient: Well, I still manage to stay in my home, so I do try to keep up with things, but... I suppose I have been putting off things that used to be routine. I actually stopped teaching my craft classes recently. I used to teach crocheting down at the community center on Thursday afternoons. We had a lovely little group, mostly ladies from the neighborhood. We were working on these beautiful afghans, the granny square kind. \n\nMy grandmother taught me how to make a granny square when I was just a little girl. She had this enormous wooden crochet hook, it looked almost like a magic wand to me back then. She lived in a drafty old farmhouse, so she was always making blankets. Thick, heavy wool ones that smelled a little bit like sheep and cedar chips. I remember she had this big cedar chest at the foot of her bed where she kept all the finished ones. It had these intricate carvings on the front, little flowers and vines. I always wondered who carved it. Probably my grandfather, he was very good with his hands. He built a birdhouse once that looked exactly like a miniature Swiss chalet, complete with tiny little window boxes...\n\nOh, I'm sorry, my mind is just wandering everywhere today. Finances, you asked. I rely a lot more on reminders now, and I've missed some calls and appointments, and family tasks I used to handle carefully. But I'm still in my house, managing as best I can.\n\nDoctor: Do you need someone else to help you with everyday tasks at home?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, I am still managing to stay in my home by myself. I don't have a nurse or a housekeeper or anything like that. But I suppose I do put off the things that used to be routine around the house. \n\nI used to be so particular about keeping a tidy home. Every Monday was laundry day, rain or shine. If it was a nice breezy day, I'd hang all the bedsheets out on the clothesline in the backyard. There's really nothing quite like the smell of sheets dried in the sunshine, is there? They just smell so crisp and fresh when you bring them in. We had this huge oak tree right near the clothesline, and sometimes the blue jays would sit up on the lower branches and scold me while I was pinning up the pillowcases. Blue jays are such bossy birds. We had a neighbor, Mrs. Higgins, who had a terrible time with them at her bird feeder. She tried putting out safflower seeds because the young man at the hardware store told her the jays wouldn't eat them, but they just threw them all out onto the lawn in a huff. The squirrels ended up getting completely fat off them instead. Squirrels are such clever little things, aren't they? They actually figured out how to lift the heavy metal lid right off her garbage can...\n\nOh, listen to me rattling on about Mrs. Higgins' garbage. You were asking if I need help with tasks. No, I don't have anyone come in. Like I mentioned with the bills, I just rely a lot more on my written reminders to get through the day, since I've been letting things slip—like those appointments and family tasks I used to handle so carefully. But I'm still managing on my own.\n\nDoctor: Can you tell me where we are right now?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, of course, we're right here in your office at the clinic. It's a very nice building, though the waiting room is just a bit drafty. I was looking at the magazines out there on the little glass table while I was waiting, and I noticed you have some copies of Reader's Digest. I haven't seen one of those in ages. I used to have a subscription, oh, back in the eighties, I think. I always loved that section with the jokes, Laughter the Best Medicine. Arthur, my late husband, he used to read those little jokes out loud to me while I was making breakfast. He had such a wonderful, booming laugh, it would just fill up the whole kitchen. We had this lovely little yellow Formica table with chrome edges, very popular back then. I would be frying up eggs, sunny side up for him, scrambled for me, and he'd be chuckling away at the magazine. We always got our eggs from a local farm stand down the road. The man who ran it, Mr. Miller, he had a glass eye. It was fascinating, really, though I always tried my very best not to stare. He lost it in the war, I believe. The Navy, maybe? Or the Army...\n\nOh, goodness, I'm doing it again, aren't I? Just drifting off. But yes, to answer your question, we are at your medical office.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost weight without trying?\n\nPatient: Well, my eating has gotten all turned around lately. That's actually part of what made me come in, to be honest. I haven't really been checking the scale to see if I've lost weight, but some days I just forget lunch completely. And then other days, I'll just stand right there at the kitchen counter eating crackers and sweets, even though nothing really tastes right to me anymore. \n\nSpeaking of crackers, I used to always buy those little square ones in the red box, the Saltines, you know? They were just perfect for my homemade chicken noodle soup. I used to make a big pot every Sunday during the winter. My mother taught me how to make the egg noodles from scratch. You just need flour, eggs, and a little pinch of salt, and you roll the dough out so thin you can almost see through it. We had this heavy wooden rolling pin that belonged to my great-aunt Martha. She lived out in Pennsylvania, near Amish country. We visited her once when I was a teenager, and we took a ride in a real horse-drawn buggy. The horse was a beautiful dapple gray named Buster. He absolutely loved peppermints. We bought a whole bag of those little red and white striped candies at the general store just for him. The store had these wide wooden floorboards that creaked every time you took a step, and it smelled like roasted coffee beans and saddle soap...\n\nOh, dear me, I'm wandering off again, aren't I? Buster and the peppermints... I'm sorry. You were asking about my weight. But yes, my eating is just all out of sorts right now, skipping meals or just snacking on things I don't even really enjoy.\n\nDoctor: Have you had less appetite lately?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, my appetite is just... it's just all turned around. That's really what made me finally make an appointment to come in. I just don't have that natural hunger telling me it's time to eat. Some days I'll look up at the clock and realize it's three in the afternoon and I've completely forgotten to have lunch. \n\nI used to have such a reliable internal clock for meals. Noon on the dot, my stomach would start rumbling. I always liked a nice egg salad sandwich for lunch, with just a little sprinkle of paprika on top. My mother used to grow her own paprika peppers in the garden, little red things that looked like Christmas ornaments hanging on the bushes. She'd dry them out in the sun on these old wooden screens. We had this big vegetable garden behind the house, right next to the neighbor's property line. The neighbors had this enormous golden retriever named Barnaby who would always dig under the fence and try to steal our tomatoes. He was a sweet dog, though, always wagging his tail so hard his whole back half would wiggle. His owners, the Hendersons, they bought him this bright blue collar with little silver bones on it. Mr. Henderson worked at the post office, and he'd always bring us our mail right to the door instead of leaving it in the box...\n\nOh, goodness, listen to me going on about the mailman. I'm sorry. But yes, my appetite is just gone. And then, like I said, other times I'll just stand right there at the kitchen counter eating crackers and sweets, even though nothing tastes right to me anymore. It's just very strange.\n\nDoctor: Have these thinking and memory problems been gradually getting worse over time?\n\nPatient: Well, I... I don't really think I'm having memory problems. Not like you're saying. I mean, everyone forgets a name here and there, right? Or walks into a room and wonders what they went in for. But I don't feel like it's getting worse.\n\nThough, speaking of memory, I was trying to remember the name of that actress just the other day. The one with the beautiful auburn hair who was in all those lovely old musicals. Maureen O'Hara! That's it. My sister Evelyn and I used to go to the picture show every Saturday afternoon to see her. It only cost a dime back then, can you believe it? A shiny silver dime. We'd get a little paper bag of popcorn to share, and it was always so salty it made my lips pucker. The man who ran the projector, Mr. Gable—no relation to Clark, of course, though we always giggled and pretended he was—he had this very thick mustache that twitched when he talked. He used to wear these suspenders with little green shamrocks on them. Evelyn asked him about them once, and he told us his grandfather came over from County Cork during the potato famine. They crossed the ocean on a ship called the... oh, what was it called? The Star of something? Or maybe it was a bird name, like the Pelican...\n\nOh, dear me. I'm doing it again. The ship... But no, to answer you, I don't think my memory is getting worse at all. I just get a little sidetracked sometimes.\n\nDoctor: Has your daughter ever had to take over paying your bills for you?\n\nPatient: Well, no, she hasn't had to take over the checkbook or anything like that. I still manage to stay in my home just fine. Though I suppose I do rely a lot more on her little reminders these days, and I put off things that used to just be routine for me. I've missed some calls and appointments lately, and family tasks I used to handle so carefully. I even stopped teaching my craft classes. \n\nI used to teach a lovely decoupage class at the community center on Tuesdays. We made the most beautiful memory boxes. You just take an old wooden cigar box—Mr. Abernathy at the corner store used to save them for me. He smoked those big thick cigars that smelled like cherry wood and molasses. He had this magnificent silver lighter that clicked so loudly you could hear it from the other aisle. He said he bought it in Paris after the war. Oh, Paris... I've never been, but my cousin Betty went for her honeymoon in 1968. She brought back this little snow globe with the Eiffel Tower inside, but the water had leaked out on the airplane ride back, so the little plastic snowflakes just stuck to the bottom of the glass. She kept it on her mantelpiece anyway, right next to this heavy brass clock that chimed every quarter hour...\n\nOh, dear. I'm wandering off again, aren't I? Betty's snow globe... I'm so sorry. You were asking about my bills. No, my daughter doesn't pay them, I just... I just let things slide a bit more than I used to, and I need a few more reminders to get things done.\n\nDoctor: Has your daughter told you that you repeat yourself or get confused more than you used to?\n\nPatient: Well, no, she hasn't said anything like that to me. I don't think I'm getting confused. I mean, we talk on the phone every Sunday evening, just like we always have. She calls right after dinner. Usually, I'll make a nice roast chicken on Sundays, with carrots and those little pearl onions. My grandmother taught me how to roast a chicken so the skin gets perfectly crispy. She used to rub the whole bird down with butter and this special sage she grew in her kitchen window. She had these beautiful terracotta pots lined up on the sill, painted with little blue flowers. My grandfather bought them for her at a flea market in Boston. He used to take the train into the city every weekend to look for antiques. He found this gorgeous grandfather clock once, but it wouldn't fit in the back of his truck, so he had to hire a neighbor with a bigger flatbed just to get it home. The neighbor, Mr. Sullivan, he had this old Ford that backfired so loud it sounded like a gunshot...\n\nOh, my goodness. I'm doing it again, talking about Mr. Sullivan's truck. I'm so sorry. What were we saying? Oh, right, my daughter. No, she hasn't mentioned me repeating myself or being confused. We just have our nice Sunday chats.\n\nDoctor: Do you still enjoy the things you used to like doing?\n\nPatient: Well, I suppose the honest answer is no, not really. I used to look forward to so many things, you know? My watercolor class, the quilting circle, my Wednesday book club... but now, I'll pack my things up, and I often just leave the bag sitting right by the front door. I just can't make myself care enough to actually go. \n\nMy quilting bag is this lovely heavy canvas tote. My niece Sarah brought it back for me when she took a trip up to Maine. Oh, Maine is supposed to be just breathtaking in the autumn. She stayed in this little coastal town—Camden, I think it was. They had a room in a bed and breakfast with a big wrap-around porch and these beautiful white wicker rocking chairs. Sarah said the lady who ran it made blueberry pancakes every single morning. She had to put this green netting over the bushes because the robins would come and eat them all before they were even ripe. There was this one robin with a little crooked beak, and he would just sit on the wooden fence post and squawk at her while she watered the plants. She used this old galvanized metal watering can... it had a big dent on the bottom from when my brother Tommy dropped it on the concrete driveway when we were little...\n\nOh, my stars. But yes, like I said, I just leave my bag by the door these days. The interest just isn't there.\n\nDoctor: Have you needed someone else to start handling your bills for you?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was saying before, nobody has actually taken over the bills for me. I rely a lot more on little reminders from my daughter, and I put off things that used to just be routine. I've missed some calls and appointments lately, and family tasks I used to handle so carefully... and like I mentioned, I even stopped teaching my craft classes at the community center. \n\nThose classes were always on Tuesdays. I bought it at a little boutique downtown that closed years ago... they used to wrap everything in this lovely lilac tissue paper before they put it in the bag. My father's silver dollar... I'm so sorry, doctor. You asked about my bills again. But yes, I still handle them, I just... I'm just not as careful with things as I used to be.\n\nDoctor: Because of your thinking or memory, have you had to stop driving?\n\nPatient: Well, no, I haven't had to stop driving. I still have my car, and I drive myself when I really need to. It's a Buick. A LeSabre. My husband bought it for me right before he passed. He always loved Buicks. Said they rode like you were floating on a cloud. He used to wash it every Saturday morning, right out there in the driveway, with a big yellow sponge and a bucket of warm soapy water. He'd always use Palmolive dish soap, the green kind, because he said it cut the grease on the hubcaps better than anything else. He'd scrub those hubcaps until you could see your face in them. He was so particular about his cars. Before the Buick, we had this old station wagon with the wood paneling on the sides. We took the kids all the way to Mount Rushmore in that car. It was the summer of '76, the Bicentennial. The kids in the back seat were eating those red, white, and blue popsicles, the Bomb Pops, and my son dropped his right on the upholstery. It left this awful sticky red stain that never did come out, no matter how much carpet cleaner I used on it... \n\nOh, for heaven's sake. Listen to me. The Bomb Pops and the station wagon. I apologize, doctor. My mind just wanders off like a loose balloon. You were asking about driving. No, I haven't had to stop because of my memory or anything like that. I just don't go out as much as I used to.\n\nDoctor: In the past few months, has any bill gone unpaid because you forgot to take care of it?\n\nPatient: Well, no, not completely unpaid, but like I was saying earlier, I do rely on my daughter to remind me about them. I haven't lost the house or anything... I still manage to stay here, thank the Lord. But I just put things off. It's like I mentioned before, I've missed calls and appointments, and those family tasks I used to be so careful with. I even stopped teaching my craft classes at the community center. \n\nI really miss the community center sometimes. The floors there were this polished linoleum, always smelled a bit like lemon wax and old paper. The janitor, Mr. Henderson, he must have been eighty years old if he was a day, but he pushed that big wide dust mop up and down the halls every single afternoon. He wore these navy blue coveralls with his name embroidered over the pocket in red thread. My husband had a shirt with his name on it like that when he worked at the hardware store. It was a bowling shirt, actually, from when they sponsored a team. The \"Hardware Hitters,\" they called themselves. They had these shiny satin jackets, bright emerald green with a big white bowling pin on the back. He brought one home for our son once, but it was miles too big. The sleeves hung down past his little hands, and he ran around the living room pretending he was a ghost...\n\nOh, my goodness. The bowling shirts. I'm so sorry, doctor. I've completely lost the thread again. You were asking about the bills. I haven't let them go completely unpaid, no, I just... I need more reminders now, and I put off the routine things."
